title: Integration architectural sync — Aurora Data / Redwood
summary: Discovery focused on integration patterns for hosted vs dedicated vs private deployments. Primary concerns: SDK compatibility with LangChain/LlamaIndex, gateway/proxy patterns, rate limiting/quotas, and hooking into Redwood observability (traces, token-level cost). Customer emphasized security (SSO, KMS) and offline/on-prem constraints for PII workloads.
topics: Rate limits and quotas per route
Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
next_steps: Redwood: share LangChain + LlamaIndex sample repo (Samir) by 2025-04-14
Aurora: provide anonymized traffic profile and token distribution spreadsheet by 2025-04-11
Schedule SE-led proof-of-concept kickoff (30d window) — tentative 2025-04-21
action_items: Samir Patel: prepare LangChain + LlamaIndex quickstart repo and a small demo notebook; due 2025-04-14
Priya Kapoor: export weekly request/response size histogram and 95th percentile latencies; due 2025-04-11
Maya Chen: send pricing banding for hosted vs dedicated with committed monthly throughput examples; due 2025-04-10
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-04-07 15:30 PDT | Duration: ~48 minutes | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Aurora), Liam O'Connor (Aurora), Daniela Ruiz (Aurora)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, Maya from Redwood. Thanks for making time. Quick audio check?
[00:07] Priya Kapoor: Yep, all good on my end. Thanks for fitting us in.
[00:10] Liam O'Connor: Good afternoon, Maya, Samir. Excited to dive in.
[00:14] Maya Chen: Awesome. Quick agenda — we wanted to understand your integration surface, how you're planning to use SDKs or "LangChain", what gateway/proxy patterns you have, and any quotas or observability hooks you need. Then we'll map that to hosted vs dedicated vs private. Cool?
[00:26] Priya: Sounds good. We'll start with a bit of context — Aurora builds a data access platform, lots of semi-structured customer transcripts, some PII. We're evaluating Redwood because we need predictable latency and want to integrate with existing LangChain-based pipelines.
[00:38] Samir Patel: Great, thank you. Liam, can you describe the current pipeline — where do inference calls originate, are you using an internal gateway, and what libraries?
[00:47] Liam: Sure. Most calls are generated by our ingestion workers and a handful of product features in the UI. We use a custom API gateway — it's Kong-based — that handles auth and basic rate-limiting. For model orchestration, our team standardizes on LangChain and LlamaIndex for retrieval-augmented generation. We also have a lightweight internal SDK that wraps requests with tenant metadata.
[01:10] Daniela Ruiz: And from security: anything that touches PII has to either be processed on-prem or be encrypted with our KMS and strict retention rules. So private deployment or dedicated with VPC peering are the main options.
[01:22] Maya: Makes sense. Two quick clarifications: when you say "LangChain", are you using the open-source Python stacks, and do you expect to call Redwood directly from those clients or through your gateway?
[01:32] Liam: Open-source Python. Ideally we'd like to keep calling through the gateway for tenant auth, quotas, and observability consistency. But we also want low latency for certain routes, so we'd consider allowing direct calls from internal services for high-QPS paths.
[01:45] Samir: Ok, so a hybrid: gateway for control plane and direct calls for performance-critical flows. Redwood supports both — our SDKs can run server-side and we also have recommendations for proxy headers and token routing.
[01:56] Priya: Can you expand on SDKs? We have some existing wrappers — do we need to rip them out to use Redwood?
[02:02] Samir: No. Our SDKs are thin; most customers either use the Redwood SDK or call the REST API. For LangChain and LlamaIndex we have connectors: a LangChain LLM wrapper and a LlamaIndex client adapter. Typically we provide sample code that shows either calling Redwood via your gateway with forwarded auth headers, or calling Redwood directly from a service with short-lived tokens minted by your gateway.
[02:23] Liam: Short-lived tokens — is that supported? We rotate keys frequently.
[02:27] Maya: Yes, we support short-lived API tokens via our control plane or you can integrate your own STS / KMS-based token creation. For Dedicated/Private, you can integrate with your internal KMS for key material if you want no plaintext keys outside your environment.
[02:40] Daniela: On observability — we need token-level cost attribution and per-route latency traces hooked into our existing datadog/tracing stack. How does Redwood expose that?
[02:48] Samir: We emit per-request telemetry and have webhooks for streaming traces. There are three options: 1) push pre-aggregated metrics to a metric endpoint, 2) send full per-request events to your S3 or log endpoint, or 3) use our tracing integration which can forward spans to your tracing backend. There's also a token-level cost breakdown in the Console and an API to pull cost attribution.
[03:11] Priya: Which option introduces the least latency? We can't have tracing slow down 95th percentile.
[03:16] Samir: The tracing path is async — spans are emitted post-response; default path adds negligible latency. Prefix/KV cache hits are served in-runtime and are the main latency optimizers, not tracing.
[03:27] Liam: You mentioned KV cache — how would that work with our gateway if we want certain prompts cached across tenants?
[03:33] Samir: Caching can be configured per-model/per-route. We support prefix caching and tenant-scoped caches. If you want cross-tenant caching you'd need to opt-in and ensure no PII is cached; otherwise caches are namespace-isolated by tenant id or by hashed key. We also have TTL controls.
[03:48] Priya: OK that's critical. Also, about the gateway/proxy pattern — we want to keep rate limiting and quotas at the gateway level but also have Redwood enforce per-customer quotas to prevent a noisy tenant from exhausting capacity. How do you recommend we split responsibilities?
[04:00] Maya: Common pattern: do coarse-grained throttling at the gateway (burst smoothing, basic rate limits) and let Redwood enforce hard quotas per API key/token and enforce usage-based routing policies. That way, your gateway protects upstream and we protect capacity on the model side.
[04:15] Liam: Is that enforced via API keys or do you support forwarded headers for tenant-id so you can map requests to quotas?
[04:21] Samir: Both. We recommend issuing per-tenant API keys (short-lived) and also accepting forwarded tenant headers if you need to do request attribution while still using a single shared key for internal services. Attribution is configurable in the Console.
[04:34] Daniela: For compliance, we need audit logs showing which user triggered requests touching sensitive data. Is that available in Dedicated/Private only or also for Hosted?
[04:42] Maya: Hosted offers audit logs too with enterprise retention + SSO integration. Dedicated and Private give you more control: logs can be routed into your S3 or SIEM and are kept in your VPC. For the highest compliance, Private on-prem gives you full control.
[04:56] Priya: Let's talk about latency targets. We have a 200ms P95 target for short form completions. Can Redwood meet that?
[05:02] Samir: It depends on heavy model and sequence length. For smaller open models on Dedicated with colocated GPUs you can hit sub-200ms P95 for 256-token-ish prompts. Hosted in our closest region may be close but depends on route and tenant isolation. For strict SLOs, Dedicated with pinned capacity is recommended.
[05:21] Liam: If we go Dedicated, how does scaling work? We expect bursty traffic from nightly ETL jobs and steady traffic from product features.
[05:29] Maya: Dedicated supports autoscaling policies and burst pools. You can set a baseline reserved capacity for steady traffic and enable burst pools for spikes. There's an option for priority-based routing so critical routes get served first.
[05:41] Priya: Back to connectors — you said you have a LangChain wrapper. Will that work with our retrieval-augmented setup using LlamaIndex?
[05:49] Samir: Yes, we have both LangChain and LlamaIndex adapters. For RAG we recommend streaming responses and using our embeddings APIs for vector indexing. We provide sample notebooks that show building a Retriever with LlamaIndex pointing at your vector DB and then passing context to the LLM via the LangChain wrapper.
[06:05] Liam: For embeddings — we run our own vector DB. Any problems if we compute embeddings via Redwood and store vectors on our side?
[06:12] Samir: That's a common pattern. You call the embeddings endpoint, store vectors in your DB. Make sure your retention policy for raw text matches compliance. Embeddings are deterministic-ish per model/version — we recommend pinning model versions in the request to avoid vector drift.
[06:26] Priya: Model pinning — is that supported by the API? We want reproducible embeddings across runs.
[06:30] Maya: Yes, you can specify model_version in each call and Redwood will honor it; you can also pin a route in the Console so your integration keeps consistent model routing.
[06:39] Liam: On the gateway side, we prefer to maintain all auth and token minting. What's the recommended flow for minting short-lived Redwood tokens?
[06:46] Samir: Two patterns: 1) Your gateway mints short-lived tokens using a service account key stored in your KMS and passes them to services; 2) Use an internal STS to request tokens from Redwood's control plane via a mutual-TLS service account. Both are supported. If you need non-exposure of keys, Private deployments can integrate directly with your KMS.
[07:03] Daniela: Any gotchas for mTLS or mutual auth?
[07:06] Maya: For Private/Dedicated in a VPC, we support mTLS and private links. For Hosted, we support mutual-TLS for enterprise customers and private peering options. You do need to coordinate certificate rotation policies.
[07:18] Liam: Performance testing — we want to run a benchmark comparing our existing internal FL-based model and Redwood-hosted model for latency and cost. Do you have a benchmarking harness or spreadsheet template?
[07:27] Samir: Yes, we have a benchmark kit: a script that can replay representative traffic, JSON schemas for payloads, and a cost calculator that maps token counts to cost bands. We'll share that kit. For Dedicated we can also run an on-prem microbenchmark if you want to push GPUs.
[07:42] Priya: Great. About quotas — can we set per-route and per-tenant quotas, and can those be enforced in real-time?
[07:50] Samir: Yes. We support hard quotas with enforcement and soft quotas with alerts. Enforcement is near-real-time; you can also configure throttling and fallback policies (e.g., degrade to a smaller model or return a rate-limited response).
[08:03] Maya: Note: fallbacks are a common way to keep UX intact during spikes — route to a cheaper or smaller model and surface a degraded badge in the app.
[08:11] Liam: How much engineering effort to integrate the wrappers into our LangChain flows? Our current wrapper expects an LLM class with a specific interface.
[08:19] Samir: Our LangChain wrapper implements the standard LLM interface and supports streaming generation, token callbacks, and stop-sequences. You should be able to swap in our wrapper with minimal changes. We'll provide a migration guide showing the exact method signatures.
[08:32] Priya: On observability again — we want trace IDs passed through the stack so we can correlate product traces to LLM requests. Is that possible?
[08:38] Samir: Absolutely. You can pass an X-Trace-Id header or our SDK auto-instruments to pull trace context. We can also emit trace ids in the response headers for correlation.
[08:48] Maya: Quick question for compliance from Daniela — if a model is hosted in Redwood Hosted but you enable "no retention" for a route, do we still have logs or are they purged?
[08:57] Daniela: (interjects) sorry that's for Redwood to answer.
[09:00] Samir: Good question. For Hosted we have configurable retention policies per-route; you can set no-retention and we will not persist request/response bodies beyond ephemeral processing, though we may still emit aggregate metrics. For strict requirements, Private gives you full control.
[09:12] Priya: What's the path for PII detection before caching or logging?
[09:16] Samir: We have optional pre-processing hooks where you can run a regex or a small classification check in-line. You can also configure the gateway to scrub or redact fields before forwarding to Redwood.
[09:27] Liam: About rate limiting on the gateway + Redwood — if a request is rejected by Redwood due to quota, does it return a specific code we can handle for fallback?
[09:34] Samir: Yes, we return structured error codes; e.g., 429 with a body that indicates quota type and suggested retry-after. Our SDK exposes typed exceptions for that so your fallback logic can respond programmatically.
[09:44] Maya: Let's talk about a simple integration diagram I want to propose: your UI and workers call your Kong gateway; gateway attaches tenant id and mints a short-lived Redwood token (or forwards header); Redwood routes requests to hosted/dedicated/private based on policy. For high-QPS internal services, they call Redwood directly with service-minted tokens. Thoughts?
[10:04] Priya: That's pretty much what we had in mind. One question: is it possible to do per-route model selection in the gateway so some endpoints always hit a smaller cheaper model?
[10:13] Samir: Yes, you can set route tags and Redwood routing policies that map tags to model families. You can also use dynamic routing rules based on token budgets, latency SLO, or feature flags.
[10:24] Liam: If we set per-route model families, can we also get per-route cost estimates before execution?
[10:30] Maya: We can provide estimated token counts and a cost estimation API; the Console also shows per-route token breakdowns historically. For real-time, our SDK can request an estimate call prior to generating the full prompt.
[10:42] Daniela: From security, are there any third-party data processors inside Redwood's Hosted path? e.g., do you use any external logging providers that might see plaintext?
[10:50] Samir: Hosted uses our managed control plane; logs can be routed to customer endpoints on request. We don't ship raw payloads to third-party analytics without customer permission. For strict needs, Dedicated/Private ensures all logs stay in your VPC.
[11:04] Priya: Good. A few nitty-gritty items: 1) We need SSO + SCIM for user provisioning; 2) We need RBAC for team roles; 3) We need an audit trail of who modified routing policies.
[11:18] Maya: Hosted enterprise includes SSO (SAML/OIDC) and SCIM; RBAC and policy audit are part of the Console. Dedicated/Private adds the option to store audit logs in your SIEM.
[11:29] Liam: Pricing: what's the delta between hosted and dedicated? Ballpark numbers?
[11:33] Maya: Ballpark: hosted is pure usage-based with tiered pricing per token/embedding. Dedicated starts with a base monthly reservation for capacity (committed spend) plus usage overage and is more predictable at scale. We'll send an example pricing band tailored to your expected throughput in the follow-up.
[11:48] Priya: One more operational question — how do you recommend rolling model updates for us? We want canarying and an easy rollback if outputs degrade.
[11:56] Samir: We have rollout controls in the Console: model version pinning, canary percentage, A/B test features, and automatic fallback to previous version if quality metrics degrade. Integration with evals can trigger alerts for regressions.
[12:09] Liam: Great. What about SDK language support? We use Python but plan a small Go microservice.
[12:15] Samir: Official SDKs for Python, Node, and Go (beta). But for LangChain your needs are in Python and that's fully supported. Go SDK supports REST patterns and streaming.
[12:25] Priya: Are there sample patterns for proxying streaming responses through Kong? Kong tends to buffer responses, which breaks streaming.
[12:33] Samir: Kong's default behavior buffers — common workaround: use a streaming-aware plugin or route streaming endpoints via a passthrough path that bypasses buffering. We'll share a Kong config snippet we've used with other customers.
[12:46] Maya: Quick callout — some transcription in tooling may confuse "KV cache" with "K V cash" (laughs) — we'll share docs with the exact term.
[12:55] Liam: (laughs) Noted.
[12:58] Priya: Ok, let's sketch next steps. We want: a) LangChain + LlamaIndex sample repo to try a quick swap; b) benchmark kit + cost spreadsheet; c) a short security packet for our compliance team about Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private; and d) tentative POC kickoff next week.
[13:17] Maya: We'll do that. Samir will own the sample repo and benchmark kit. I'll send pricing and the compliance packet.
[13:24] Samir: I'll also prepare a Kong streaming config snippet and a short demo notebook showing token callbacks and trace id propagation.
[13:33] Daniela: One ask from our side — can Redwood's logging anonymize user identifiers in logs before they reach storage? We have strict PII rules.
[13:41] Samir: Yes, we have configurable scrubbing and redaction rules; we can apply regex or structured field scrubbing pre-ingest. We'll include redact examples in the security packet.
[13:51] Priya: Timeline-wise, if we like the quick integration, we want a 4–6 week POC with ~2 weeks of integration + 2–4 weeks of load testing. Is that feasible?
[14:02] Maya: Absolutely feasible. We'll tailor the POC plan after we see your traffic profile.
[14:08] Liam: Any blockers regarding our VPC setup? We have peering to AWS us-west-2.
[14:12] Samir: We can peer into us-west-2 or set up private link. For Dedicated we'll provision endpoints; for Private we can deploy in your VPC if desired.
[14:21] Priya: Alright, let's recap action items and owners.
[14:24] Maya: Samir will share the LangChain + LlamaIndex sample repo, Kong config snippet, and benchmark kit by 2025-04-14. Maya will send pricing and compliance packet by 2025-04-10. Priya will share traffic profile by 2025-04-11. Tentative POC kickoff week of 2025-04-21.
[14:45] Liam: Thanks, everyone. This was very helpful.
[14:48] Priya: Thanks.
[14:50] Maya: Thanks — we'll follow up in email with the links.

End of transcript.

Notes on transcription: Some technical terms may be mis-transcribed (e.g., "KV cache" as "K V cash"). Speaker labels are mostly accurate but may have small attribution errors.
